Basically, the ideal situation in economics is called "Perfect Competition". Essentially, this prevents any one firm from dominating a market (gaining "market power"), and it delivers the best quality products to buyers, for the most reasonable prices.

In this context however, firms are perpetually frustrated. They can't get an edge. So, what they do, and have done, is they get the government to provide them that edge. They lobby for regulations which hurt opposing industries/firms or benefit them, or tax loopholes, or patents, or generally create barriers to entry into their field. As a result, they can get ahead of other competition, and even get an oligopoly or permanent monopoly.

None of this happens in the context of a limited government. Natural monopolies can form, but they do not last long, and they typically provide a product that is niche, and again, not for long.

I'm an aspiring hobbyist astronomer, where do I start?
Get a nice pair of 10x50 binoculars and a star chart. If you can put them on a tripod that really helps. Learn the constellations, the brighter deep space objects, and the planets. Read, read, read.

When I was into it I would read Sky and Telescope and Scientific American. Nowadays I get my brief exposure to contemporary astronomy on the internet. I've been following the Pluto mission and before that they had those great photos of the comet.
